title: Enhancing disease coping and quality of life through digitally integrated psycho-oncological care: the COPE-WELL study
summary:
Many people with cancer experience symptoms during drug-based cancer treatment. Common symptoms include severe tiredness/exhaustion (fatigue), nausea, and gastrointestinal problems. These symptoms can place a heavy burden on everyday life and significantly reduce quality of life.
Psycho-oncological support (i.e., help with emotional and psychological burdens related to cancer) can help patients cope better with the illness and treatment side effects. However, there is not always enough time or enough specialized staff available to provide this support.
That is why the COPE-WELL study is developing a digital support program: a website with videos and helpful information that can be used easily—independent of time and place. This program is intended to complement usual care and help relieve pressure on existing services.
We also know that people cope with cancer in different ways. Some remain more active and optimistic, while others feel more helpless or hopeless. These differences can influence how symptoms are perceived and how well supportive interventions work. It is still not well understood whether a digital program has different effects depending on a person’s coping style.
What is the research question?
The study aims to find out whether using the website can help patients improve their quality of life and perceive side effects and symptoms as less burdensome while receiving cancer treatment with cell-damaging (cytotoxic) medication.
What happens at the beginning (screening and study start)?
Before the study starts—and before participants are randomly assigned to a group—we check:
•	whether a person meets the requirements for participation,
•	whether the person agrees to take part (written informed consent), and
•	what the baseline situation is at the start.
This includes, for example:
•	age and sex/gender,
•	information about the disease and planned treatment,
•	whether using a smartphone/tablet/internet is feasible,
•	questionnaires on quality of life and symptoms (some may already be completed at the first visit).
How is use of the website evaluated?
To assess whether the program works well in everyday life, we also look at:
•	how often and how long the website is used,
•	how many videos or modules are viewed,
•	whether participants are able to “stick with it” (i.e., whether many contents are actually completed),
•	how the content is rated (easy to understand, helpful, relevant),
•	whether someone stops using the program—and, if they choose to share it, why.
This information is used to improve the program and tailor it more closely to patients’ needs.
How many participants are planned?
The study compares two groups:
•	one group uses the website in addition to usual care,
•	the other group receives usual care without the website.
To reliably detect a difference, around 160 participants are needed (80 per group). Because some participants may drop out over time (e.g., due to hospital stays or withdrawal from the study), the study aims to include about 190 participants in total.
Participants are assigned to the groups at random (1:1). Where possible, care is taken to ensure that the groups are comparable, for example with regard to study site and sex/gender.
How will we evaluate whether the website helps?
All participants complete questionnaires at specific time points, for example:
•	at the beginning,
•	after 6 weeks,
•	after 12 weeks,
•	and later during follow-up assessments.
We then compare how quality of life and symptoms change in both groups. In addition, we explore:
•	whether people with different coping styles benefit differently,
•	whether there is a link between “more use” and “stronger effects,”
•	how participants’ overall feedback on the website looks.
conditions: Acute leukaemia of unspecified cell type
Malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung
Malignant neoplasm of kidney, except renal pelvis

interventions.name:
Arm A (Intervention):
Standard care + COPE-WELL website (video-based psycho-oncological intervention). PROs: FACT-G, EORTC QLQ-C30, FACIT-Fatigue, MAT, GSRS at T0, week 6, week 12, week 24, week 36; MAC (coping) at T0. In addition, usage/adherence metrics and brief module ratings (intervention arm

Arm B (Control):
Standard care (no digital intervention). PROs: FACT-G, EORTC QLQ-C30, FACIT-Fatigue, MAT, GSRS at T0, week 6, week 12, week 24, week 36; MAC (coping) at T0.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adult oncology patients (≥18 years)
First-line therapy
Treatment including cytotoxic agents
ECOG performance status 0–1
Sufficient proficiency in German
Written informed consent provided
Exclusion criteria:
No second primary malignancy
No known psychiatric disorder
Exclusion of patients receiving immunotherapy only (i.e., without cytotoxic systemic therapy)
No relevant visual or hearing impairment that would preclude study participation or use of the intervention
